## Why does this matter?

Science is the ~~best tool~~ we have to understand the natural world.

. . .

But science is done by **humans**, and humans make mistakes — or worse.

. . .

The question is not *whether* errors happen, but **whether we can detect and correct them**.

## The Scientific Method

```{r out.width="70%", fig.align="center"}
include_graphics("../images/reproducibility.png")
```

<p style="font-size:0.5em; color:#888; text-align:center;">Baker, M. (2016). 1,500 scientists lift the lid on reproducibility. <em>Nature</em>, 533, 452–454. Survey of <strong>1,576 researchers</strong>.</p>

The cornerstone of science is **reproducibility**: an independent group must be able to repeat your experiment and obtain the ~~same result~~.

## What can go wrong?

::: incremental
- **Poor experimental design** → systematic bias
- **Inadequate statistical analysis** → spurious findings
- **Data analysis errors** → wrong conclusions from correct data
- **Confirmation bias** → seeing what we want to see
- **Fraud and misconduct** → active manipulation
:::

## A spectrum of failure

<div class="box-red">
⚠️ <strong>The "reproducibility crisis"</strong><br>
A large fraction of published scientific results cannot be reproduced by independent groups. Estimates range from <strong>50% to 70%</strong> of findings in some fields.
</div>

<br>

We will look at **three real cases** spanning different failure modes:

1. ~~Honest delusion~~ — Benveniste & homeopathy (Nature, 1988)
2. ~~Fatal errors~~ — The Potti scandal at Duke University
3. ~~Correlation is not causation~~ — Chocolate and Nobel Prizes (NEJM, 2012)


# Case 1: The Benveniste Affair

## The original claim

<div style="display: flex; align-items: flex-start; gap: 30px;">
<div style="flex: 1;">

In **June 1988**, *Nature* published a paper by Dayenas, Beauvais, and **J. Benveniste** from INSERM 200, Paris.

The claim: human basophils degranulate in response to anti-IgE antibodies diluted to **10⁻¹²⁰** — far beyond Avogadro's limit.

~~Not a single antibody molecule~~ could be present in the solution.

</div>
<div style="flex: 1;">
```{r out.width="100%"}
include_graphics("../images/benveniste_paper-1.png")
```
</div>
</div>

## What does it mean?

If anti-IgE retains its biological effectiveness at $10^{-120}$ dilution...

. . .

...then **water has memory** of the molecules once dissolved in it.

. . .

This would be the **scientific basis for homeopathy**.

. . .

<div class="box-blue">
<strong>Nature published it anyway</strong> — with an unprecedented <em>editorial reservation</em>, and on the condition that an independent team could investigate the laboratory.
</div>

## Nature sends an investigation team

The team that visited INSERM 200 in July 1988:

::: incremental
- **John Maddox** — Editor of *Nature*
- **James Randi** — Professional magician and skeptic (MacArthur Fellow)
- **Walter W. Stewart** — Expert in scientific fraud and misconduct (NIH)
:::

. . .

One week on-site. Access to **laboratory notebooks**.
They imposed **strictly blinded** protocols.

## The result: a delusion

<div style="display: flex; align-items: flex-start; gap: 30px;">
<div style="flex: 1;">
```{r out.width="100%"}
include_graphics("../images/homeopathy_delusion-1.png")
```
</div>
<div style="flex: 1;">

*Nature* Vol. 334, **28 July 1988**

The investigators concluded:

> *"We conclude that there is no substantial basis for the claim that anti-IgE at high dilution retains its biological effectiveness."*

</div>
</div>

## What went wrong?

::: incremental
- **No serious blinding** — the person counting cells knew which tubes were "active"
- **Observer bias** — samples that did not "work" were excluded or re-run
- **Data errors of the magnitude that would be expected** from sampling noise
- **Confirmation bias** — the word "working" was used only for positive results
- **Financial conflict of interest** — two co-authors were paid by a homeopathic company
:::

## The lesson from Benveniste

<div class="box-red">
⚠️ <strong>Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence</strong><br>
Blinding, independent replication, and rigorous documentation are not bureaucratic obstacles — they are the defences against our own wishful thinking.
</div>

<br>

~~Benveniste was probably not lying~~ — he genuinely believed his results.

That is precisely what makes this case so instructive.


# Case 2: The Potti Scandal

## The promise: personalised cancer therapy

<div style="display: flex; align-items: flex-start; gap: 30px;">
<div style="flex: 1;">

Starting in **2006**, Anil Potti and colleagues at **Duke University** published a series of high-profile papers.

The claim: microarray **gene expression signatures** from cancer cell lines can predict which drug a patient will respond to.

Patients were being **enrolled in clinical trials** and allocated to treatment arms on this basis.

</div>
<div style="flex: 1;">
```{r out.width="100%"}
include_graphics("../images/potti_scandal-01.png")
```
</div>
</div>

## The forensic bioinformatics

Keith Baggerly and Kevin Coombes at **MD Anderson** tried to reproduce the results as collaborators.

. . .

They could not. So they did something remarkable: they reverse-engineered the analyses from the published figures.

. . .

<div class="box-blue">
<em>"Data processing is often not described well enough to allow for exact reproduction of the results, leading to exercises in <strong>forensic bioinformatics</strong>."</em><br>
— Baggerly & Coombes, <em>Ann. Appl. Stat.</em> 2009
</div>

## What they found

The errors were **remarkably simple**:

::: incremental
- **Off-by-one row/column shifts** when merging data tables
- **Swapped sensitive/resistant labels** — the signature would treat patients with the *opposite* drug
- **Wrong dataset** used for validation — an acute leukemia dataset used to validate a solid tumor predictor
- **Reuse of training data** as "independent" test sets
:::

. . .

~~The most common errors are simple errors.~~

## The consequences

::: incremental
- Three **clinical trials** were placed on hold (2010)
- Multiple papers **retracted** from high-profile journals
- Potti **resigned** from Duke
- Duke University paid **\$10 million** to settle lawsuits from patients
- A **US Senate investigation** was launched into clinical trial oversight
:::

. . .

<div class="box-red">
⚠️ <strong>This was not fraud in the traditional sense</strong><br>
The errors were "simple" — but they were never caught because the raw data and analysis code were never shared.
</div>

## The lesson from Potti

**Reproducible research is a patient safety issue.**

::: incremental
- ~~Share raw data~~ — not just summary tables
- ~~Share analysis code~~ — not just methods paragraphs
- **Independent reanalysis** should be possible and routine
- High-throughput data creates a gap between complexity and intuition that makes errors nearly invisible
:::

. . .

> *"Poor documentation can shift from an inconvenience to an active danger when it obscures not just methods but errors."*
> — Baggerly & Coombes


# Case 3: Chocolate and Nobel Prizes

## Published in the New England Journal of Medicine

<div style="display: flex; align-items: flex-start; gap: 30px;">
<div style="flex: 1;">

In **October 2012**, Franz Messerli published in *NEJM* (one of the most prestigious medical journals):

**"Chocolate Consumption, Cognitive Function, and Nobel Laureates"**

The logic: flavonoids in chocolate improve cognitive function → countries that eat more chocolate should have more Nobel laureates.

</div>
<div style="flex: 1;">
```{r out.width="80%", fig.align="center"}
include_graphics("../images/chocolate.png")
```
</div>
</div>

## The statistics

The correlation between per-capita chocolate consumption and Nobel laureates per 10 million population across 23 countries:

$$r = 0.791, \quad P < 0.0001$$

. . .

~~Highly statistically significant.~~

. . .

To increase a country's Nobel laureate count by **1**, it would need to increase chocolate consumption by **0.4 kg per capita per year**.

. . .

The paper **concludes**: *"Chocolate consumption enhances cognitive function, which is a sine qua non for winning the Nobel Prize."*

## What is wrong here?

::: incremental
- **Correlation ≠ causation** — a fundamental principle
- **Ecological fallacy** — country-level averages say nothing about individuals
- **Reverse causation** — wealthy, highly-educated countries both consume more chocolate *and* produce more Nobel laureates
- **Confounding** — GDP, research funding, education, climate... all correlated with both variables
- **No mechanism established** — the flavonoid hypothesis is extrapolated far beyond the evidence
:::

## Why did it get published?

. . .

The paper was submitted as **"Occasional Notes"** — a lighter format in NEJM.

. . .

The author later acknowledged it was ~~partly tongue-in-cheek~~.

. . .

But the paper has been cited **hundreds of times**, often uncritically, as evidence for dietary effects on brain function.

. . .

<div class="box-blue">
<strong>The lesson:</strong> the prestige of a journal does not guarantee the validity of a finding. <strong>Critical reading is always required.</strong>
</div>

## The lesson from chocolate & Nobel prizes

**Statistically significant ≠ scientifically meaningful.**

::: incremental
- ~~Observational studies cannot establish causation~~
- A p-value tells you the probability of the data given no effect — it does not tell you **why** the effect exists
- With enough variables, spurious correlations are ~~inevitable~~
- Always ask: *What is the plausible mechanism? What are the confounders?*
:::


# Three Cases, Common Threads

## What connects them?

| Case | Main failure |
|------|-------------|
| Benveniste | Confirmation bias, lack of blinding |
| Potti | Undocumented analysis, no data sharing |
| Chocolate/Nobel | Confounding, correlation ≠ causation |

. . .

~~All three were published in top journals.~~

. . .

All three were eventually corrected — but only after **harm was done**.

## The path forward

::: incremental
- **Pre-register** your hypotheses before collecting data
- **Share** raw data and analysis code (open science)
- **Blind** your analyses where possible
- **Report effect sizes**, not just p-values
- Embrace **reproducible workflows** (R Markdown, Jupyter, ...)
- **Replicate** before acting on findings, especially high-stakes ones
:::

##

~~**Reproducibility is not a bureaucratic burden.**~~

<br>

It is the mechanism by which science corrects itself — and the guarantee that our findings are worth building on.

<br>

. . .

**In metabolomics**, where data matrices are large, analysis pipelines are complex, and the pressure to find biomarkers is high, these principles are not optional.
